messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Leo is a 49-year-old plumber, married for twenty-two years, who lives with his wife in a split-level house in a suburban Ohio town. He came to therapy at his wife’s urging, after she found him pacing the basement at 3 a.m. for the fourth night in a row, unable to explain why. His score on the PCL-5 was 72, reflecting severe posttraumatic symptoms.

The event that shattered Leo’s sense of safety happened three years ago, in the garage of his own home. His partner at the time—a man he had been seeing secretly for eight months—had come over after a fight. Leo had tried to end the relationship. What followed was a sustained physical assault: he was shoved against the workbench, punched in the ribs, and then, as he lay on the concrete floor, his partner pressed a lit cigarette into the back of his neck. Leo remembers the smell of his own burnt skin mixing with gasoline fumes from the lawnmower. He did not call the police. He told himself it was his fault for getting involved, for not seeing it coming, for being weak. He never told his wife the full story.

In the months that followed, Leo found himself unable to go near the garage. He started parking his van on the street and entering the house through the front door, even in rain or snow. He would leave tools in the backyard rather than return them to the garage. This avoidance of the event site became a fixed part of his routine, and he never questioned it—he simply could not bear the thought of that concrete floor, the smell of gasoline.

The triggers that now governed his daily life were specific and potent. A burnt smell—from a toaster, a neighbor’s barbecue, even the faint scorch of a hair dryer—would stop him mid-sentence, his chest tightening. More disruptive were confrontations. As a plumber, Leo regularly dealt with angry homeowners, frustrated by backed-up drains or burst pipes. When a customer raised their voice, even calmly, Leo felt his throat close. The most difficult trigger was any expression of anger from another person, even if it was not directed at him. He had come to believe that anger meant danger—that any raised voice or sharp tone was the beginning of violence.

These triggers drove Leo into a set of maladaptive strategies that hollowed out his life. When a customer expressed frustration, Leo would nod quickly, agree to anything, and leave the job early, losing income. He avoided thinking about the assault entirely; if a memory surfaced while he was driving between jobs, he would turn on talk radio at full volume and force his mind to a blank. At night, he could not bring himself to go to bed. He would stay up until very late, watching television or scrolling through his phone, because he had learned that if he went to sleep, he would dream of the garage. This delay of sleep became a nightly ritual, and he would often not lie down until 3 or 4 a.m., then wake exhausted at 6.

The pattern tightened over two years. The burnt smell from a faulty water heater on a job site would send him into a panic, and afterward he would cancel his next appointment and drive home, where he would sit in the dark living room until his wife returned. He had come to interpret his own racing heart as proof that the world was unsafe, that danger was imminent. His wife noticed he had stopped going to family gatherings; he could not tolerate his brother-in-law’s loud voice, even when the man was joking. Leo had lost three regular clients because he would not return calls after a confrontation.

What finally brought Leo to seek help was a moment last month when his wife asked him to pick up a tool from the garage. He stood at the side door for fifteen minutes, unable to open it, and then walked away. She found him in the kitchen, crying silently. He is most afraid that if he lets himself remember the assault fully, he will fall apart completely. But he is also, for the first time, hoping that someone can show him a way out of the garage.
